Customers can tell when they are talking to a poorly implemented AI. Overly formal language, generic responses that do not address the specific question, and rigid conversation flows all create an experience that feels more frustrating than helpful. [...] Key takeaways:

 Hallucinated or inaccurate answers are the number one complaint driving customer frustration
 Poor escalation to human agents traps customers in unhelpful AI loops
 Lack of context forces customers to repeat themselves across interactions
 Rigid, scripted responses fail to address nuanced customer issues

results.title: AI‑generated complaints and how to deal with them - Care Management Matters
results.content:
### Common pitfalls providers should avoid

 Under-engaging: Some providers instinctively dismiss AI-generated complaints as less ‘real’ or less valid, focusing more on the style than the substance. This risks missing genuine concerns.
 Over-engaging: Others feel compelled to rebut every overly legalistic point. This leads to long, defensive responses that lose sight of what actually matters.
 Adopting a defensive or cold tone: The formality of AI-generated complaints can cause providers to ‘mirror’ that tone. But formality is not a substitute for empathy, which could help de-escalate matters.

Behind every complaint, even an AI-polished one, it is important to remember that there is a person who is feeling distressed, frustrated or confused.

results.title: When members use AI: handling the next generation of complaints – Sackers
results.content:
1. Don’t panic – the presence of AI-assisted content does not necessarily mean a complaint is stronger or more likely to succeed.
2. Focus on the substance – a lengthy complaint does not always equate to more legal arguments. Before drafting a response, identify the key issues that are genuinely in dispute, leaving aside any repetition.
3. Always check the law – AI models can “hallucinate” legal authorities (ie they can cite incorrect or made-up authorities that often appear plausible), misquote cases or misinterpret judgments and TPO determinations. Always verify any legal references before responding. [...] 1. Lengthy complaints – members can now simply use prompts such as “add more detail” and be provided with a five-page IDRP complaint, even where the underlying issue could be summarised in a few paragraphs.
2. Structured headings and bullet points – most AI models favour a highly structured format, often using headings, sub-headings, bullet points and bold text to present arguments.
3. Adversarial tone – complaints may increasingly rely on references to case law and statutes to support arguments, sometimes resulting in a more confrontational tone.
4. Confident assertions with limited supporting evidence – AI-assisted complaints can present arguments with a high degree of confidence, even where the legal authority or factual basis is weak, incomplete or inaccurate. [...] 5. Repetition of the same point in different ways – AI tools often expand complaints by restating the same argument using different wording. This can create the impression that multiple issues are being raised when, in reality, there may only be one or two core concerns.
